newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian protests resume, U.S. senators address crowd.
newsitem.headline: Serbian protests resume, U.S. senators address crowd.

text.p: Daily protest rallies resumed on Wednesday despite government concessions in Serbia's political crisis, with fiery rhetoric against President Slobodan Milosevic and two U.S. senators giving supportive speeches.

"We salute those people who peacefully seek democracy and work for a democratic Serbia that is ruled by law and which is at peace with its neighbours and itself," Senator Carl Levin of Michigan said after addressing several thousand protesters in central Belgrade.
Levin, senior Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, was accompanied by Jack Reed, Democrat of Rhode Island, who told the crowd: "We salute you for your brave struggle for democracy.
"You have chosen a difficult path but there is no turning back," Reed said. "Americans stand with you because you stand for democracy.

The two senators appeared before the pro-democracy crowds after holding talks with Milan Milutinovic, foreign minister of federal Yugoslavia which groups Serbia and tiny Montenegro, and with Army Chief of Staff Momcilo Perisic.
Reed said they had discussed the Dayton peace accords and the resettlement of refugees and had commended the military "on staying out of this political trouble".

It was the 59th day of protests across Serbia to force Milosevic and his Socialist government to reinstate the results of annulled November 17 municipal elections in which the opposition won 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest cities.
The demonstrators took Tuesday afternoon off after mobilising half a million strong overnight for Orthodox New Year in the biggest rally yet seen.
Electoral commissions in Belgrade and Nis subsequently announced that the victories of opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition candidates would be reinstated.
But opposition leaders remained extremely sceptical and resumed their noisy, colourful and peaceful protests.

"We want our victory in its entirety," Zoran Djindjic, the Democratic Party head and a Zajedno leader, told the crowd. "No horsetrading, Mr President. The November 17 results are sacred to the democratic opposition...
"Things are beginning to crash down about his head," Djindjic added. "We don't believe that it is a matter of any sensible politics on their part, they're panicking...
"People gripped by panic are dangerous and that's why we must be cautious."
Vuk Draskovic, another leader of the tripartite Zajedno coalition and head of the Serbian Renewal Movement, said victory was close but the opposition must remain vigilant.
"We have never been closer to achieving the electoral victory (but) ...we are dealing with a regime prepared for everything," Draskovic said.
He said the reinstatement of the opposition victories in the capital Belgrade and Nis, Serbia's second biggest city, "could be a new trick on their part, a new ploy to buy time.
"Nothing is finished, let's wait three more days," Draskovic added, referring to time limits for appeals that Socialist hardliners could lodge against the decisions.
Riot police set up a cordon in front of the roughly 3,000 demonstrators but protesters for the most part stayed clear of them and policemen made no attempt to intervene.
